en: The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, appended to the Record of the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha under the Music Tree, together with a great [assembly].
The assembly of bhikṣus numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty, their names renowned throughout the ten directions, having exhausted all fetters and attained liberation;
the eight classes of spirits and deities likewise aspired to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
Śāriputra rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha is the Dharma King; according to the inclinations of sentient beings, he expounds the teachings of the Dharma in various ways, causing devas and humans to respectfully uphold them—some hear them through hearsay, while others practice or do not practice.”
"What is meant by one who practices the Dharma?
What is meant by one who does not practice the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are able to ask such a question on behalf of all sentient beings.
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.”
Now, those who practice the Dharma include those who uphold it through direct hearing and those who uphold it through hearsay; all such are called the Saṃgha.

For example, when the bhikṣu Ratthapāla heard the Buddha’s teaching that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," he immediately contemplated arising and ceasing, thereby severing all outflows (*āsrava*).
"Truly, my disciples are those who practice the Dharma.

As for those who merely hear it—such as the bhikṣu Kāyadassī—he heard you say, and he heard Kālodayin say: 'Drinking alcohol opens the door to negligence and creates a great obstacle for one who is practicing the Path.'"
He immediately entered the *araṇā-samādhi* and attained the vision that severs the origin [of suffering].

Those who practice my Dharma do not practice what is non-Dharma; those who practice what is non-Dharma are said to be "not practicing. Such people are non-practitioners of the Dharma and not my disciples; they have entered the dense forest of false views.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way, World-Honored One, are the precepts spoken by you for the bhikṣus sometimes opened and sometimes closed?
For instance, when you provided a meal for the householder Sutanu who had suddenly risen [to offer hospitality], you prohibited the bhikṣus from eating breakfast."
Just as when invited by the people of Śrāvastī, he was permitted to eat rice along with fish and meat;
yet when invited by the people of the village of Piṇḍava, he was not permitted to eat rice but only thin gruel;
and when invited by King Bimbisāra, he was again permitted to eat his fill of rice and food.
Just as when, at the request of Cchandakaśrī, [the Buddha] permitted eating several times over at many households,
yet none were allowed to eat their fill— how should future bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās uphold such words?
The Buddha said:
"That which I have spoken is called 'according to the occasion.
Within this particular time, one should employ these words; within that particular time, one should employ those words. For the sake of effective practice, all should be upheld."
I shall seek nirvana; Mahākāśyapa and the others shall together provide detailed instruction and serve as a great reliance for the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, no different from me.
Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda; Ānanda, in turn, transmitted it to Madhyāntika; Madhyāntika, in turn, transmitted it to Śāṇavāsa; and Śāṇavāsa transmitted it to Upagupta.
After Upagupta, there was King Śakrāditya, who propagated the Sūtras and Vinaya throughout the world. His grandson, named Puṣyamitra, succeeded to the legitimate throne and consulted his ministers:
"How can I ensure that my name and deeds shall not perish?"
At that time, a minister said:
"There are only two matters. What are these two?"
It is just as when former kings constructed eighty-four thousand stupas and surrendered all the wealth of their kingdoms to make offerings to the Triple Gem;
this is the first instance.
If it were otherwise, one would have to do the opposite—destroying stupas, extinguishing the Dharma, and harming the fourfold assembly of those who have stilled their minds.
"This is the second point.
Although their reputations may be good or bad, both shall remain imperishable.
The King said:
"I lack the majesty and power of my predecessors; I must establish further deeds to bring my conduct to renown.
He then commanded his fourfold army to attack the Kukkutārāma Monastery.

The monastery had two stone lions that roared and made the earth tremble; the King was struck with great terror and retreated into the city. Those among the people who witnessed this sighed and wept, filling the roads.

The king became even more enraged; not daring to enter himself, he drove and coerced his generals and soldiers to commit acts of death and injury at will, and strictly commanded that the seven assemblies—monks (*bhikṣu*), nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), male novices (*śrāmaṇera*), female novices (*śrāmaṇerī*), female probationers (*śikṣamāṇā*), as well as renunciants and female renunciants—all be assembled.
Question: "Is it better to destroy a stupa?
Or is it better to destroy a dwelling?"
They all said: "We pray that none of these be destroyed.
If it must be done, you may destroy only the rooms."
The king became violently enraged and said,
"How can this not be done? Thereupon, he proceeded to kill them all without distinction of age, until the flowing blood formed a river.
He destroyed more than eight hundred monasteries and stupas.
The lay devotees raised their voices in wailing and weeping in bitter distress; the king had them arrested and imprisoned, subjecting them to flogging and punishment.
Five hundred arhats ascended the Southern Mountain and were thus spared; because the mountain valleys were hidden and perilous, the military forces could not reach them.
Fearing they might not be cleansed, the King issued a bounty to various countries, offering three thousand pieces of gold for every head brought.

You, Kuntibhadra, an Arhat and one entrusted by the Buddha to propagate the teachings, manifested as immeasurable people who seized the heads of immeasurable bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs and received gold everywhere.
The king’s entire treasury was completely exhausted.

The king became even more enraged. Then, King Kuntibhaṭa manifested his body and entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Although the king personally inflicted harm upon him, he remained unharmed, sustained by the power of his concentration.

Next, the scripture platform was set ablaze; as the flames began to rise and the fire reached the scriptures, Maitreya Bodhisattva, by means of his supernormal powers, took my sutras and vinaya up to Tuṣita Heaven.
Next, they arrived at the Tooth Stūpa, where the deity of the stūpa said:
"A Yakṣa named Caraka previously sought my daughter, but I was stingy and did not give her to him.
Now that he has vowed to protect the Dharma, I shall give my daughter to him."
The messenger prostrated himself with a sincere heart.

The deity was pleased by the movement of the insect and, with his hands, lifted up a great mountain to press down upon the king and his fourfold army; they all died at once, and the descendants of the royal house were completely extinguished there.
"Subsequently, there was a king whose nature was exceedingly virtuous and kind.

Maitreya Bodhisattva manifested as three hundred youths and descended into the human realm to seek the Way of the Buddha; they received the teachings from five hundred arhats, and the men and women of the kingdom likewise went forth together to leave the household life."
In this way, the number of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs increased once again.
The arhats ascended to heaven to retrieve the Sūtras and Vinaya, returning them to the human realm.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Zǒngwén who consulted with the arhats and the king to divide my Sūtras and Vinaya and establish many towers and halls, so as to provide a place for those coming to study and inquire.

"At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who delighted in fame and frequently engaged in contentious debate. He excerpted and edited our Vinaya, expanding and enlarging what Kāśyapa had codified, naming it the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya. He further collected and synthesized what had been omitted, deceiving those who were newly learning the Dharma; he formed a separate faction and engaged in mutual disputes over right and wrong."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who sought a judgment from the king. The king assembled the two groups and had them cast black and white voting sticks, proclaiming to the assembly:
"Those who prefer the old code may take a black stick; those who prefer the new code may take a white stick."
At that time, those who chose the black ones numbered in the tens of thousands, while those who chose the white ones numbered only in the hundreds.
The king, considering them all to have been taught by the Buddha, concluded that because their preferences differed, they could not dwell together.
Those who study the old [tradition] are numerous; following this as its name, it is called the Mahāsāṃghika.
Those who study the new [tradition] are few, yet they are the Sthaviras; following the Sthaviras as its name, it is called the Tāmraśāṭīya.
As for the Mahīśāsaka school, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, due to disputes, the Sarvāstivāda and Vātsīputrīya schools will further arise.
From the Vātsīputrīya school, there further arose the Dharmottarīya school, the Bhadrayānīya school, the Sammatīya school, and the Śāṇavāsika school.
From that Sarvāstivāda school, the Mahīśāsaka school further arose.
From Maudgalyāyanopatiṣya, the Dharmaguptaka school and the Suvarṣaka school originated.
From the Haimavata school, there further arose the Kāśyapīya school and the Sautrāntika school.
Within four hundred years, the Saṃmitīya school further arose.

Within two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, due to divergent doctrines, the Mahāsāṃghika school will give rise to the Vibhajyavāda school, the Lokottaravāda school, the Kukkuḷaka school, the Bahuśrutīya school, and the Prajñaptivāda school.
During the three hundred years, due to various heterodox teachers, there further arose from these five schools the Mahādeva school, the Caitika school, and the Aparaśaila school.

After such a vast number [of schools] had circulated for a long time, whether correctly or incorrectly, only five schools remained, each highlighting its own strengths and designating the color of their robes.
The Mahāsāṃghika school, which diligently studies the various sūtras and proclaims the true meaning, resides at the center; therefore, they should wear yellow robes.
The Dharmaguptaka school, which masters the flavor of principle and leads others toward benefit, manifesting excellence, should wear red robes.
The Sarvāstivāda school, which is broad in learning, quick-witted, and skillful in guiding through the transformation of the Dharma, should wear black robes.
The Kāśyapīya school, being diligent and courageous in gathering and protecting sentient beings, should wear saffron-colored robes.
The Mahīśāsaka school, contemplating in meditation to penetrate the subtle and fully comprehend the profound mysteries, should wear blue robes.
Therefore, when the bhikṣu Rāhuṇeyya went on his almsround, he was unable to obtain food;
later, by wearing the five kinds of monastic robes alternately, he was able to obtain food in great abundance.
Why is this? It is because in his previous lives he was habitually and excessively stingy; when he saw a śramaṇa approaching, he would hurriedly close his doors and say, "The master is not at home."
"Seeing others practicing giving, he felt joy and focused his mind, vowing to become a śramaṇa.
For this reason, although he has now attained the state of a renunciant, he remains so impoverished and destitute."
"In my Dharma, those who have left the household life wear only coarse cloth and the shrouds of the deceased; it is because of Rāhuṇa that they now receive various kinds of robes.
Śāriputra said, "How is it that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata has become so fragmented in such a short time?"
"Since its original flavor has been lost, how can it be upheld?
The Buddha said, "The Mahāsāṃghika retains its pure and correct flavor; as for the other schools, they are like nectar that has been diluted."
When the devas drink it, they consume only the nectar and discard the water;
when humans drink it, they take in both the water and the nectar, whereby it sometimes cures their ailments and sometimes causes them to contract illnesses.

"It is the same for those who recite and study it: those of great wisdom are able to grasp what should be taken up and what should be abandoned, whereas the ignorant are unable to discern this. Śāriputra said:
"The Tathāgata previously stated that in cold countries, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear secular clothing and cover their heads.

When the bhikṣu Kaṇa was traveling through the village of Mahāvana, he encountered a great freezing rain during which birds and beasts had all perished. A villager gave him a secular garment, yet the World-Honored One ordered him to perform repentance."
"Why is that? The Buddha said,
"I permit you to wear dyed cloth, provided it is placed inside your robes."
Śāriputra said: "Why does the World-Honored One always say that bhikṣus must not place their bowls on the ground, but should hold them with a clean cloth?
If there is no clean cloth, they should use grass, leaves, or wood."
"Lord, the bhikṣu Śukra, together with his retinue, accepted the invitation of King Duṣkaradharman and went forth with clean boards, holding up their alms bowls.
Why did the World-Honored One revile him, saying:
'This is the conduct of an evil Māra; he is not one who practices the Dharma'?"
I said: "One uses pure objects that are not subject to defilement.
If no such pure things are available, one may use leaves from trees or grasses, discarding them immediately after a single use."
One must not use tree bark or the inner flesh of wood, because their substance inherently contains resin.
Nor should one use lacquer or varnish, as they attract dust.
Furthermore, if the material is already dried and withered, it was originally present there, and if it is moist and warm, the resin will flow again.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, why do you permit the bhikṣus to accept invitations for meals from donors as well as the regular meals provided by the Saṃgha?
Why did the Tathāgata rebuke the bhikṣu Araṇyaka for accepting an invitation for a meal from the householder Abhaya?”
"This is a man made of earth and wood;
he should not eat human food.
The Buddha said:
"By destroying the proper deportment, when eating, they merely look with their eyes and do not receive the food with their hands.
Even the non-Buddhist brahmins know how to receive it; how much more so should my disciples not fail to receive the food?"
How much more so regarding food; one must not refuse to accept any object whatsoever, with the sole exceptions of precious gems and gifts from women.
Even if one is performing a ritual, one should still offer the garment worn upon one's body.
"If one receives a vessel for storing gold, it is judged as an act of giving.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Why does the World-Honored One speak of obstructive dharmas, stating that one must not drink even as much alcohol as a mustard seed, calling this 'breaking the precepts' and 'opening the gate of negligence'?"
Regarding the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery: there was a bhikṣu who had been ill for years; his condition was critical and he was on the verge of death.
At that time, Upāli asked him, "What medicine do you require?"
"I shall seek it for you;
whether in the heavens, among humans, or throughout the ten directions, I will procure whatever is required for you. He replied:
"The medicine I require is contrary to the Vinaya; therefore, I did not seek it, which has led me to this state.
Rather than exhaust my life and limb, I cannot permit myself to violate the discipline. Upāli said:
"What medicine do you require?
He replied, "The teacher said I need five sheng of wine."
Upāli said, "If it is for the sake of illness, it is permitted by the Tathāgata.
Having obtained wine through begging, he took it and was cured.
Having been appointed, he felt ashamed and still considered himself to have violated the precepts; he went to where the Buddha was and earnestly repented his transgression.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and upon hearing it, he rejoiced and attained the path of an Arhat.
The Buddha said:
"Alcohol brings about many faults and opens the door to negligence.
Even if one drinks as little as a mustard seed, the accumulation of transgressions is already vast."
"If it eliminates the suffering of illness, it is not something that was previously prohibited.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the Tathāgata has always said that one must not kill living beings, even down to an ant?"

On the eighth day of the twelfth month, by the side of the Long Water River in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he competed in magical arts with the non-Buddhist teacher Śaila; first, he compelled him through his supernormal powers to fall into defeat, whereupon Śaila, overcome with shame, threw himself into the water and perished.
"To look on with indifference as they sink away and not rescue them—is that not killing?
Furthermore, he addressed the assembly, saying:

'Śūli held this evil dharma and deluded sentient beings; now that his past roots of goodness have matured, he has extinguished this evil body and been reborn in the Heaven of Good Vision—is that not a joy?'"

My disciples should, on this day, perform a pure ritual bathing; by washing away the impurities of the body, they eliminate erroneous views from their minds, so that as the body becomes pure, the mind likewise becomes pure.
"You resemble a hired servant; you possess neither compassion nor mercy.
The Buddha said, "O one of great wisdom!"
That you are able, for the sake of those who have not yet attained realization, to ask about this essential truth is commendable.
The Tīrthika Śūlika has accumulated false views throughout immeasurable ages and vowed to obstruct the True Dharma.
In the past, during the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I was practicing the bodhisattva path.
I came upon a village where many people suffered from leprosy and the dead lay scattered everywhere.
I gathered various medicines and provided relief as appropriate, and all were healed.

Among them was one named Wu-yin Bu-dai (Wu-yin not wearing), who was a student of the Brahmins; he prided himself on his many talents and refused to believe or submit, only seeking me out as death approached.
I said to him: "Previously you were treatable, yet you would not take the medicine;
now that your life-breath is about to end, you come seeking it again. At this moment, even medicine could not save you."
Budaire said, "I am no longer able to judge who is superior or inferior; I pray that we may decide our victory or defeat together in a future life.
If I am defeated, I shall take my own life and seek rebirth as your disciple."
"If you are not my equal, you shall become my servant.
At that time, I replied:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Therefore, he has now been born in this land to encounter me; at the end of his life, as his roots of goodness ripened, we met in accordance with our karmic affinity.
Yet, when he spoke, he lost his footing and felt ashamed before his kin, so he threw himself into the water to take his own life."
"Although his body has perished, because he gave rise to a virtuous mind, he has been born within my Dharma; since there is further progress for him, I do not rescue him.
Śāriputra asked: "In what way does the instruction command disciples to bare the right shoulder?"
Furthermore, for the people of the Kāśyapa village, he spoke the *Nagara-upama-sūtra*, saying:

"My disciples should properly don the kāṣāya, covering both shoulders so as not to expose the flesh, keeping the upper and lower edges level to manifest the appearance of a field of merit, and walking with dignified decorum."
Again he said:
"Do not reveal your inner thoughts.
Regarding these two statements, how should they be upheld?
The Buddha said:
"When performing acts of worship, one should bared one shoulder to facilitate the task.
When serving as a field of merit, one should cover both shoulders to manifest the marks of the field."
How does one practice making offerings?

When seeing the Buddha or when inquiring after the health of teachers and monks, one should perform acts according to the circumstances: whether it be dusting the bed, sweeping the floor, folding robes, arranging mats and cushions properly, making flower designs on the ground with mud, leveling high spots and filling in depressions, or sprinkling water and moving things—these are various forms of offering.
What is meant by acting as a field of merit?

When a king invites one to a meal, when one enters a village to beg for alms, when one sits in meditation, recites the scriptures, or wanders beneath the trees—people see that one is dignified and worthy of admiration.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions are the eight classes of spirits and deities born into the evil realms yet constantly hear the True Dharma?”
The Buddha said:
"By means of two kinds of karma:
first, by way of evil one is born into the evil realms; second, by way of goodness one experiences much happiness."
He asked again:
"Good and evil are two distinct things; can they ever become the same?
The Buddha said:
"It is indeed possible.
For this reason, the eight classes of spirits and deities are all called 'neither human nor non-human.

As for those who are celestial deities, they were previously human beings who, by means of carriages, palanquins, dwellings, food, and drink, made offerings to the Triple Gem, their parents, and virtuous and superior persons; yet because they still harbored stinginess, parsimony, flattery, and envy, they received the bodies of celestial deities, such as the celestial deities Puguang (Universal Radiance) and Jingsheng (Pure Excellence)."

As for the nāga deities of space, they have cultivated the roots of virtue and extensively practiced the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā); yet, because they do not rely on right mindfulness and possess a quick temper prone to anger, they receive births as humans and non-humans, such as the Nāga King Maṇiprabha and others.

As for the yakṣas, they delight in great giving; some first cause harm and later bestow benefit, and according to the degree of their merit or demerit, they dwell in the heavens, in mid-air, or beneath the earth.

As for the gandharvas, in their previous lives they were also somewhat free from anger and always delighted in practicing generosity; adorning themselves with blue lotuses and performing various musical arts, they have now become these deities who constantly perform all manner of music for the gods.

As for the asura deities, their will is stubborn; they do not follow the pure merit performed by virtuous friends, but prefer to pursue illusory and false people to perform various perverse merits. They rely on heterodox teachers and are exceedingly fond of practicing giving, yet they also delight in watching the disputes of others; therefore, they have received this present body.
As for the Kinnara gods, they previously practiced great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), yet they were constantly arrogant and looked down upon others; therefore, they have received their present bodies.

As for the Kiṃnara gods, in the past they delighted in exhorting others to resolve upon bodhicitta, but they did not rectify their own intentions and pursued various deviant practices; therefore, they have obtained their present bodies.
As for the Mahoraga spirits, they practiced giving and protected the Dharma, yet their nature was prone to anger; therefore, they have received this present body.

Whether humans or non-humans, all have done so by relying on false teachers and practicing deceitful, evil paths; using the heterodox to confound the orthodox, they each claimed it to be the Way and established themselves therein.
Now, the supramundane path is not intermingled with the deceitful and flattering speech of Māra and the heterodox;
such flattering speech does not lead out of birth-and-death, but rather causes one to enter the evil realms.
It is the kind of discourse spoken by deceitful and heterodox persons: on a grand scale it resembles the Path, yet in its subtle details it is merely a deceptive glitter.
One who relies upon the True Dharma and those who practice the True Dharma shall attain the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as liberation in the unconditioned.
If one relies upon counterfeit teachings and follows teachers of false guidance, one will be bound by birth and death, forever sinking into the evil realms.
These ignorant people do not seek transcendence from the world, but enter the net of false views.

These false guides, though they have read many scriptures, fabricate false precepts through their own perverse deeds; they produce deceitful and sycophantic teachings to delude ordinary people and seek their veneration. They speak of what they do not know, saying: "I know."
A non-human being might say: "I have attained it.
Or, someone might challenge this, saying:
"How do you know?
How do you obtain it? He replied:
"A deity of the empty realm and a spiritual friend from the netherworld secretly spoke to me," he said; or it was said:
"In such-and-such a year and month there will be benefit and harm; they revealed these signs in advance, so that one should take precautions and provide protection."
"This shall perish while that shall flourish; I shall gain while you shall lose. Thus they deceive.

These shallow and vulgar people are unable to contemplate deeply the roots of virtue; following after false and superficial matters, they lose their right view, engage in unwholesome deeds, and—while alive—covet money and silk, and upon death, enter the evil realms.
Their tongues are pulled out and they swallow molten copper for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years;
thereafter, they become animals for immeasurable ages;

they are then reborn as ghosts, dwelling in mountain forests, wildernesses, rivers, seas, or houses, constantly harboring flattery and deception without rest. They may delude and slander practitioners, causing them to lose their path, or manifest as false sorcerers, speaking in various ways to terrify people with the forms and attire of the deceased. Being utterly loathsome and base, they seek food and drink from others without end.
When my disciples who possess upright hearts and do not lose right mindfulness hear this, they immediately rebuke it and never dare to do so again.

However, if my disciples harbor weak minds and are easily distracted, they seek exemption from it; finding such an opportunity, they pursue their desires in a thousand ways and ten thousand manners, never tiring of their quest.
“Such a person lacks the marks of a true man; moved by evil, they will fall into the miserable realms after death—this is truly to be pitied.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying, “As for the eight classes of spirits and deities, do those who rely on space become space-deities, and those who rely on earth become earth-deities?”
The Buddha said:
"There are other earth deities such as Viśuddhapuṣpaprabha.

In past lives, they were fond of practicing generosity, yet they were prone to anger, difficult to satisfy, addicted to wine, and delighted in song and dance; therefore, they became these deities, wearing robes of pure white, clean and stainless."
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why did the Tathāgata tell Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Kings that 'I shall not long remain before entering parinirvāṇa'?"
Each of you shall protect and uphold my Dharma in your respective regions.
After I have passed away, the four great bhikṣus—Mahākāśyapa, Piṇḍola, Kuntapanta, and Rāhula—shall remain in this world without entering parinirvāṇa to circulate my Dharma.

The Buddha said: "However, during the era of the Image Dharma, the faculty of faith is weak and thin; although one may give rise to faith, it cannot be firm, and thus one cannot move the disciples of the Buddhas."

"Though you have practiced with single-minded devotion for many years, it is not equal to a single moment of goodness during the Buddha’s lifetime; its utmost sincerity is such that there is no longer any duality of direction.

You shall serve as a witness to his faith. According to the depth or shallowness of his practice, manifest for him the image of the Buddha or the image of the Sangha—whether through voices from the air, the appearance of radiance, or even within dreams—and cause his resolve to become firm. When Maitreya descends to be born, he will permit you to enter Nirvana."
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In the twenty years prior to the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, he ordained various disciples; there was no fixed time for giving, but rather he gave as the occasion arose.”
"After twenty years have passed, one gives many fixed objects as offerings.
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said:

"There was a son of a householder named Bhinnavatara, who, having cultivated roots of goodness in past lives, was born into a brahmin family and desired to leave the home life to cultivate the unsurpassed path."
Following Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he went to the Devavatiya Monastery in Pāṭaliputra to seek full ordination.
Maudgalyāyana said to him:
"You should repent of your past transgressions for seven days and seven nights, so that they may all be purified."
"If there are no obstacles, I shall request [the robe] for you from the Saṃgha. Puṇṇa said:
"How can it be known that the obstacles have already ceased?"
"How may I know that I have received the precepts?
I pray that all Buddhas will bestow their majestic spiritual power upon me, so that my transgressions may be extinguished and I may perceive the signs of having received the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"Simply be diligent and sincere; when your sincerity reaches its peak, you will see it for yourself.
Pindola replied to the Buddha, "I respectfully accept your venerable instruction."

Thus, with sincere and poignant earnestness day and night until the fifth evening, various objects rained down within his chamber—whether towels or cloths, fly-whisks or brushes, knives or axes, awls or shovels—falling one after another before his very eyes.
Then, having given birth to a mind of joy and a mind of attaining the fruit,
after seven days had passed, I reported this in full to Maudgalyāyana.
Maudgalyāyana questioned me, and I said to him:

"These are objects for removing dust and wiping away defilements; they should be offered as a *dakṣiṇā* (gift) to the preceptor, for he is the one through whom the conditions [for ordination] were fulfilled.
Now, regarding those who receive the precepts, they may offer whatever they are able to provide according to their means; it is not limited to these items, nor is it necessary to possess them all.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There are donors who have constructed monasteries and provided them with abundant provisions and offerings. Yet in future ages, there will be monks who merely resemble those who have left the household life; they will come at improper times to the stewards of food and request meals to eat.”
"What kind of offense does the one who gives and the one who eats incur?
And what kind of merit does the original donor obtain?
The Buddha said:
"One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts; such a person is a thief.

One who gives food at an improper time is likewise a person who has broken the precepts and is a thief; by taking the property of a donor when it was not given, one commits the offense of taking what is not given."
"It is not the fault of the donor; the donor incurs no demerit.
Although the object has been lost, there remains the merit of having generated the intention to establish it. Śāriputra said:
"If one receives food at the proper time and eats it at the proper time, but does not finish it and then eats again at an improper time;
or if one receives it at the proper time but eats it at an improper time—
would one still obtain merit?"
The Buddha said:

"Those who eat at the proper time are pure; they are the field of merit, they are the renunciants, they are the Saṃgha, they are the true friends of gods and humans, and they are the guides of gods and humans."
That which is impure is like violating the precepts; it is a great theft and constitutes the abode of hungry ghosts and the dwelling place of sin.
To solicit at improper times means to grant [the gift] at whatever time—whether appropriate or inappropriate—one pleases.

This distributor of food is called one who has retreated from the Path; he is called an evil Māra; he is called the three evil realms; he is called a broken vessel; he is a leper, for he destroys the fruits of goodness and lives by means of theft and begging.

For this reason, the various Brahmins do not eat at improper times, and even the non-Buddhist brahmacārins do not eat in an illicit manner; how much less, then, should my disciples—who know the Dharma and practice the Dharma—act in such a way?
All such as these are not my disciples; they are thieves who steal the benefits of my Dharma and are attached to the dharma of non-existence.
They are thieves of fame and thieves of food—persons of unrighteousness.

If one steals and gives, or if one receives—even a single lump, a single pinch, a slice of salt, or a slice of vinegar—one dies and falls into the Hell of the Scorched Intestines (*Taptāntra-naraka*), where one must swallow glowing iron balls.
Upon emerging from that hell, one is reborn among pigs and dogs, consuming all manner of impurities.
Furthermore, they are reborn as evil birds, whose cries people find strange;
later, they are reborn as hungry ghosts, dwelling within monasteries or inside latrines, where they consume excrement and filth for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
If one is reborn among humans, they will be poor and lowly, despised and loathed by others, and whatever they say will not be trusted by people.
This is worse than stealing a single person's property, for the latter’s offense is still relatively light.
"Because they have robbed many people of their wealth, because they are excellent fields of merit, and because they have severed the path to transcendence.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Many of the Tathāgata’s own kinsmen have left the household life; did they do so out of their own spontaneous resolve?"
"Is this through the Buddha's supernatural power?
The Buddha said, "The Śākyas are arrogant and attached to pleasure; how could they have the aspiration for it?"
It was specifically by the decree of my father, the King, that among the members of the royal clan who have fathered two sons, one son must follow me.

Ānanda, having long accumulated roots of goodness and being deeply devoted to the True Dharma, has come to where I am with the Śākya youths Bāhula, Nandika, Kambala, Nanda, Upananda, Ānanda, Devadatta, and Upāli; having bathed and purified themselves, they have come seeking to leave the household life.
At that time, there was an elder named Vīraṭa, who separately ordained Ānanda and Ānanda.
Next, there was an elder named Vāśula, who separately ordained Devadatta and Upananda.

Only Ānanda has cultivated the dhyāna of non-forgetfulness and mastered dhāraṇī through his past practice; within a short time, he attained the Buddha-awakening samādhi, gathering the waters of a million rivers to form rain, which then rushed down and flowed into the great ocean.
Ānanda took it from the sea with his hand and distinguished it; its color and flavor were unmixed, and he returned it to its original source without any loss.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Śāriputra,” the Tathāgata has often said, “is foremost in wisdom among the śrāvakas; it was not thought that one of such narrow mind could inquire into this essential meaning.
The Buddha continued, “He has long planted the seeds of clear awakening and has propagated my Dharma, benefiting sentient beings through his various sharp faculties of wisdom.”
"How is it that the Tathāgata says the kindness of one's parents is so great that it must not go unrequited, yet also says the kindness of one's teachers and preceptors is immeasurable?
Which of these is the greatest?"
The Buddha said:

"As for those who live at home, they serve their parents with filial piety while remaining in their presence; yet there is no repayment for their upbringing that can equal it, for it is because the kindness of giving birth and raising them is so profound that it is called 'great'."
If one studies under a teacher to develop insight and knowledge, the teacher’s kindness is great indeed.

For those who leave the household life, it is by the power of the teacher that they abandon their parents’ home of birth and death, enter the gateway of the Dharma, and receive the subtle and wondrous teachings.
"It nurtures the Dharma-body, produces the wealth of merit, and sustains the life of wisdom; no service is greater than this, and to pursue its source is merely secondary.
He further asked:
"By what name should this sutra be called?"
The Buddha said:
"It shall be titled 'The Parables Asked by the Bodhisattva,' because it is vast and extensive.
It shall also be titled 'The Questions of Śāriputra.'"
At that time, having heard this teaching, fifty newly ordained bhikṣus established the faculty of faith and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The long-established virtuous ones, as well as the devas, nāgas, and the other eight classes of beings, were all greatly rejoiced; they paid homage and departed.
